title: Minimizing the stabbing number of matchings, trees, and triangulations
contribution: SODA 2004 extended abstract (read as arXiv cs/0310034v1): sketched NP-hardness proofs for minimum-stabbing matchings, spanning trees and triangulations; an LP with weakly polynomial lower bounds and a planar-support heavy-edge theorem (at least 1/5 for matchings, more than 1/3 for trees) for iterated rounding; and the computational study the journal version D001 dropped (CPLEX 8.0 LP, IP and iterated rounding on 62 axis-parallel matching instances).
problem_entry: An item of the Demaine-Mitchell-O'Rourke list of 30 open problems. Earlier work gave extremal bounds and applications, but no complexity results or conjectures, no good combinatorial lower bounds and no approximation beyond O(sqrt n) from Welzl; Mitchell pushed the authors to take it on (abstract, pp. 1-2, 12).
key_idea: Hardness first, then one LP for three jobs: polynomial-time lower bounds (ellipsoid method), a heavy fractional edge for Jain-style iterated rounding, and exact or near-exact solutions with the simplex method and integrality. Stabbing rows break Jain's 1/2 lemma (Fig. 7), so the authors use a different fact: some optimal fractional solution has planar support, which gives an edge of at least 1/5 (matchings) or more than 1/3 (trees) (pp. 2-3, 8-10).
assumptions: Binary edge variables on the complete straight-line graph of a planar point set plus a common bound k; one row per representative stabbing line (O(n) per direction, O(n^2) directions); Edmonds' blossom rows for matchings, cut rows for trees; n made even by dropping a point if necessary; the LP results need no general position, the hardness proofs use collinear points; instances from TSPLIB, Solomon C-class, grids and random points (pp. 3, 7-8, 10).
proof_devices: 3SAT reductions with collinear barrier gadgets that use up the stabbing budget (Theorem 3.1, p. 3; Lemmas 3.3-3.4, pp. 4-5)
the decision threshold 5 rules out any factor below 6/5 (Corollary 3.1, p. 4)
perturbation by powers of epsilon, from axis-parallel lines to all directions (Corollary 3.2, p. 4)
pigeonhole over the 2x2 cycles of a crossing-number barrier (Lemma 3.5, p. 5)
triangle count between two rows of points (Lemma 3.6, p. 5)
sweep argument: the stabbing number changes only at a vertex, so O(n) lines per direction and O(n^2) directions suffice (p. 8)
weakly polynomial LP solution by the ellipsoid method with polynomial-time blossom separation (p. 8)
planar support of some optimal fractional solution by an uncrossing 2-exchange argument, proof deferred (Lemmas 5.1-5.2, p. 9)
a planar graph has a vertex of degree at most 5 and at most 3n-6 edges, giving heavy edges of 1/5 and more than 1/3 (Theorem 5.1, p. 9)
iterated rounding: fix a heaviest edge to 1 and re-solve; the number of fractional edges falls each round (p. 10)
experiments: CPLEX 8.0 LP and IP on a Pentium III 700 MHz, 1 GB, Linux, four-hour IP limit; 62 axis-parallel matching instances (10 TSPLIB up to 442 points, 16 Solomon C-class, 25 grids, 11 random); per row the LP value and time, the IP optimum or incumbent and time, and the rounding value; no competing method; 16 rows hit the limit, and the five odd TSPLIB instances are infeasible but CPLEX does not detect it (pp. 10-12). My count: the rounding value is within a factor 1.93 of the LP bound on every row; on the 46 rows with a proven optimum it equals the optimum on 19 and is within 20% on 41.
positioning: Answers an Open Problems list item that earlier work had met only with extremal bounds (Welzl, Matoušek, de Berg and van Kreveld, Shewchuk), calling itself 'the first general algorithmic study'; extends Jain's iterated rounding where its lemma fails, and links the LP class to the EGRES budgeted-matching open problem (pp. 2, 8-9).
writing: Extended-abstract register: an 'Our results in detail' bullet list, proof sketches with full details deferred, heavy hedging on the approximation ('should imply', 'appear to be', 'We are hopeful'), but unhedged empirical sentences that extend to trees. The heavy-edge constants are consistent here (p. 2 and Theorem 5.1, p. 9), unlike D001 p. 2 per its card. The introduction only promises to 'hint at' a hardness proof for tree crossing numbers, yet Theorem 3.2 states it without qualification (pp. 2-3, 5, 10).
limits_future: Proofs are sketches; the constant-factor guarantee needs an extra argument because the objective is a max, and it remains the main open problem; hardness needs collinear points; only axis-parallel matchings are computed, with prototype code. Future work: the approximation proof, small constant stabbing numbers (Theorem 7.1), the average stabbing number as minimum length (Theorem 7.2), stabbing-independent subsets, and more computations in the full paper (pp. 3, 10, 12).

method_links.note: Step 6, with failures reported: the text states 'preliminary results', calls the code 'prototypes', marks the rows that hit the limit, reports that CPLEX misses the infeasibility of the odd instances, and counts the one-shot heuristic's single exception.

Checkpoint: 'often', 'typically' and 'mostly within about 20%' come without counts. The tables back them (my count: 41 of the 46 rows with a proven optimum within 20%, worst case 5 against 3 on rand50a; 28 of 33 if the identical c1xx and c2xx rows count once).

Step 6: the claim of better-than-guarantee quality for 'factors of 5 or 3' covers spanning trees, which were not computed, and calls factors guarantees although they are unproven. D001 drops the computations but keeps the sentence, pointing to an experimental report (D001 pp. 3, 23).

Exit B: the constant-factor guarantee stays labelled as open ('should imply', 'appear to be', 'We are hopeful'); the late 'bad moves' and the one-shot approach are offered as observations still to evaluate.
Step 5 only: the conclusion lists the open questions, with two small theorems.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Existing candidate (D001). Here the same LP also gives the exact and near-exact solutions of the computational study.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: first exact IP in a theory-dominated area
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Existing candidate (D001): 'the first general algorithmic study of stabbing problems', with IP optima on 46 of the 62 rows.

transferable: Give each instance one table row with the LP bound, the heuristic value, and the IP optimum, or its incumbent written as an upper bound when the time limit stops the IP, so that every heuristic value carries its own gap certificate (Tables 1-2, pp. 10-11).

Trace the LP value along the iterations of a rounding heuristic to see where quality is lost (lin318: about 100 iterations, LP value above 9.000 only in the last ten, ending at 11 against an LP bound of 8.113; p. 12).
When every LP point is a convex combination of integral structures, try one-shot rounding: a maximum-weight integral structure on the LP support graph, compared with iterated rounding (p. 12).

For a min-max objective over an infinite family of probes, use a sweep argument (the count changes only at a vertex) to keep O(n) lines per direction and O(n^2) directions; points that share coordinates shrink the row set further (pp. 8, 10-11).

When a known rounding lemma fails under side constraints, show the LP where it fails, then prove a structural property of some optimal solution (planar support, by uncrossing) and read a heavy variable off a counting bound (Fig. 7 and Theorem 5.1, p. 9).

Screen instances for trivial infeasibility before a long IP run and keep infeasible ones out of the tables: five odd TSPLIB instances ran four hours in CPLEX 8.0 without the infeasibility being detected (p. 12), despite the paper's own rule to drop a point (p. 3); summing the degree equations (2 sum x = n) already excludes odd n (this parity check is mine, not the paper's).

quotes.text: The stabbing number obtained from iterated rounding is often very close to the LP lower bound, and in our experiments it is never off the optimal value by more than a factor of 2; typically, it is much better, and mostly within about 20% of the optimum.
Even though our prototypes are not yet ready to solve even larger instances, they may serve as a good starting point for the development of an industrial strength code.
